items.hook: Before you approve the next big project, declare it dead.
items.body:
Gary Klein's premortem, published in Harvard Business Review in 2007: gather the team after the plan is ready, announce that it is a year later and the project has failed badly, and ask everyone to write down why.

The trick rests on a 1989 study by Mitchell, Russo and Pennington. Imagining an event as already past raised the number of reasons people could generate for it by about 30 percent.

I ran this before a plant expansion. The polite risk register had six items. The premortem produced twenty, and the one that nearly happened, a port delay on imported machinery, came from the youngest engineer in the room.

Approval meetings reward optimism. The premortem gives doubt a legitimate place to stand.
items.question: When did a project fail for a reason someone in the room already knew?

card.title: The premortem
points: Plan is ready, not yet approved
Announce: one year on, it failed
card.stat_label: more reasons found when the failure is imagined as past
card.source: Klein, HBR 2007; Mitchell, Russo and Pennington, 1989

items.facts: Klein 'Performing a Project Premortem' HBR 85(9) 2007; Mitchell, Russo, Pennington 1989: ~30% more reasons generated (quantity, not accuracy)

items.hook: Sales wants a 5 percent discount to close the quarter. Here is what it costs.
items.body:
Marn and Rosiello's study of pricing in Harvard Business Review, 1992: for the average company, a 1 percent price cut removes about 11 percent of operating profit. A 1 percent rise in volume adds only about 3 percent.

The arithmetic is simple. A price cut falls straight through to profit. Extra volume carries its own variable cost with it.

So that 5 percent discount has to bring a very large volume increase just to stand still, and the customer who got it will expect it next quarter too.

Before agreeing: ask what the discount buys that a payment term, a bundle or a delivery promise could not. Most of the time the answer is nothing but a quieter sales meeting.
items.question: What is the standing discount in your business that nobody has questioned for years?

card.title: Price beats volume
points: 1 percent price cut: about 11 percent of operating profit
Offer terms, bundles or service first
card.stat_label: of operating profit lost to a 1 percent price cut, average company
card.source: Marn and Rosiello, HBR Sept to Oct 1992

items.facts: Marn & Rosiello 'Managing Price, Gaining Profit' HBR 1992: 1% price cut wipes 11.1% of operating profit for the average company; 1% volume ~3.3% per secondary coverage

items.hook: A study of 758 consultants found AI made them better at some tasks and worse at others. Nobody could tell which from the outside.
items.body:
Harvard and Boston Consulting Group ran a field experiment in 2023. Consultants with access to GPT-4 completed 12 percent more tasks and finished them 25 percent faster, with higher rated quality, on creative and analytical work inside the model's range.

On a business problem that sat just outside that range, the same people with the same tool performed 23 percent worse than colleagues working alone.

The authors called it the jagged frontier. Tasks that look equally hard to a human can fall on opposite sides of what the machine can do.

For a finance team: AI drafts the commentary, the policy, the first analysis. The judgment call on whether the number is right stays with the person whose name is on the report.
items.question: Which task did you hand to AI that it quietly got wrong?

card.title: The jagged frontier
points: Inside the frontier: more, faster, better
Outside it: worse than working alone
The edge is invisible from outside
Keep judgment where your name sits
card.stat_label: worse on the task outside the frontier
card.source: Dell'Acqua et al., Harvard Business School working paper, 2023

items.facts: Dell'Acqua et al 2023, 758 BCG consultants: +12.2% tasks, 25.1% faster, higher quality inside frontier; 23% worse on the outside task

items.hook: One ship blocked one canal for six days and held up about 9.6 billion dollars of trade every day.
items.body:
March 2021. The Ever Given wedged across the Suez Canal. Lloyd's List estimated 9.6 billion dollars of goods were held up each day it stayed there. Roughly 12 percent of world trade passes through that canal.

Factories in Germany waited for parts. Retailers in India waited for containers. Freight rates moved before anyone had a plan.

Then, in 2024, the Red Sea attacks sent ships around the Cape of Good Hope instead, adding seven to ten days to Asia to Europe transit.

The lesson for anyone who plans inventory: your supplier's reliability is not the risk. The route is. If one waterway, one port or one truck road sits between you and your material, you are carrying that risk whether you have priced it or not.
items.question: How many days of stock would you survive if your main route closed tomorrow?

card.title: When the route is the risk
points: Suez: about 12 percent of world trade
Red Sea 2024: seven to ten extra days
Price the route, not only the supplier
card.stat_label: of trade held up per day, Lloyd's List estimate
card.source: Lloyd's List, 2021; carrier advisories, January 2024

items.facts: Ever Given 23-29 Mar 2021, ~6 days; Lloyd's List $9.6bn/day; Suez ~12% of global trade; Red Sea 2024 Cape rerouting +7 to 10 days

items.hook: India has more than 7.9 crore registered small enterprises and a formal credit gap of 20 to 30 lakh crore rupees. I learned what that gap feels like from one shopkeeper in Lagos.
items.body:
He had no word for working capital. He knew which customer paid late, which supplier would wait, and exactly how much cash the shop needed to open on Monday.

Every evening he counted three things: what he sold, what he bought, what he spent. That was the whole of finance, before we dressed it in vocabulary.

The Udyam registry counted over 7.9 crore micro, small and medium enterprises by March 2026. Studies for RBI and SIDBI put their unmet formal credit need between 20 and 30 lakh crore rupees. Banks say they cannot see the numbers. Shopkeepers say the forms are not written in their language.

ScoreMyBiz exists because those two statements are the same problem. If a shop can show its three daily numbers cleanly, somebody can lend against them.
items.question: What would it take for a bank to trust a shop that keeps its books on a phone?

card.title: Three numbers a shop already knows
points: Credit gap: 20 to 30 lakh crore rupees

card.source: PIB, Ministry of MSME, 2026; RBI Sinha Committee; SIDBI studies

items.facts: PIB May 2026: 7.9 crore enterprises registered (4.72 cr Udyam + 3.21 cr Udyam Assist) as of March 2026; RBI Sinha committee gap Rs 20-25 lakh crore; SIDBI/Crisil 2025 gap Rs 25-30 lakh crore

items.hook: Nine out of ten large transport projects run over budget. The planners were not stupid. They were looking inward.
items.body:
Bent Flyvbjerg studied 258 transport infrastructure projects across the world. Nine in ten exceeded their cost estimate, with an average overrun of 28 percent.

Daniel Kahneman tells the story from the inside. His team estimated a textbook would take about two years. A colleague who knew similar projects admitted that most took seven to ten years and about 40 percent were never finished. The book took eight.

That is the planning fallacy, and its cure is the outside view: before trusting your own schedule, look at what happened to the last twenty projects like yours.

I now ask one question in every capex review. Not "how long will this take?" but "how long did the last three take, and what makes us different?" Usually nothing does.
items.question: What did your last big project cost against its first estimate?

card.title: Take the outside view
points: Ask how similar projects actually went
Expect the average overrun, not zero
Explain why yours is different, in writing
If you cannot, use the base rate
card.stat_label: transport projects over budget, average overrun 28 percent
card.source: Flyvbjerg, 258 projects; Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

items.facts: Flyvbjerg et al: 258 transport projects, 9 in 10 over cost estimate, avg overrun 28%; Kahneman curriculum anecdote: ~2 year estimate, ~40% of similar never finished, took ~8 years

items.hook: A 10 percent discount at a 30 percent margin needs 50 percent more volume just to earn the same money.
items.body:
The arithmetic nobody does in the sales meeting.

Gross margin 30 percent. Give away 10 points of price and the margin on each sale drops to 20. To earn the same gross profit you must now sell 30 divided by 20, which is one and a half times the volume.

At a 20 percent margin, the same discount needs double the volume. At 15 percent, triple.

So the question to the sales team is never "will the discount help?" It is "do you believe this customer will buy 50 percent more because of it?" Said out loud, the answer is usually no.

Keep this table on your wall. It ends more bad decisions than any policy document.
items.question: What margin does your team think it is discounting from, and what is it really?

card.title: The discount table
points: 30 percent margin, 10 percent off: sell 1.5 times more
Ask: will they really buy that much more?
card.stat_label: volume needed to break even on a 10 percent discount at 30 percent margin
card.source: Arithmetic: original margin divided by new margin

items.facts: arithmetic: margin m, discount d -> volume multiple m/(m-d); 30/20=1.5, 20/10=2, 15/5=3

items.hook: The first large field study of generative AI at work found the biggest gains went to the least experienced people.
items.body:
Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond followed 5,179 customer support agents at a software company after an AI assistant was introduced.

Issues resolved per hour rose 14 percent on average. For novice and low-skilled agents the gain was 34 percent. For the most experienced, almost nothing, and in a later version of the paper a small dip in quality.

The assistant was effectively spreading the habits of the strongest workers to everyone else.

For a finance department this changes where to deploy first. Not with the senior analyst who already knows the ledger. With the new joiner doing reconciliations and first drafts, where the tool shortens the learning curve by months.
items.question: Who on your team would gain most from an AI assistant tomorrow: the expert or the newest hire?

card.title: Who gains from AI
points: Deploy where the learning curve is steepest
card.stat_label: productivity gain for novice workers, versus 14 percent average
card.source: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, NBER working paper 31161, 2023

items.facts: NBER w31161 (2023): 5,179 agents, +14% issues/hour avg, +34% novice/low-skilled, minimal for experienced; 2024 draft 15% avg, small quality decline for most experienced

items.hook: In January 2024, 354 container ships were sailing the long way round Africa. If you import, that was your lead time changing without asking you.
items.body:
Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea pushed carriers to avoid Suez. By early January 2024 Linerlytica counted 354 container vessels diverted around the Cape of Good Hope, about 16 percent of the world fleet.

The detour added seven to ten days to Asia to Europe transit. Spot rates from Shanghai to Rotterdam rose 115 percent in weeks.

What this did to a finance plan: safety stock built for a 30-day lead time now covered 20. Working capital tied up in transit rose with the voyage. Landed cost moved while list prices stayed put.

The response is not panic buying. It is three numbers on one page: lead time today, stock cover in days, and the freight share of landed cost. Review them monthly, not when the news forces you.
items.question: Do you know your freight share of landed cost today, or only the one in the budget?

card.title: Three numbers for an import business
points: Lead time, today not last year
card.stat_label: days added by the Cape detour, Asia to Europe
card.source: Linerlytica, January 2024; Drewry World Container Index

items.facts: Linerlytica early Jan 2024: 354 container ships rerouted via Cape, 4.65m TEU, 16.4% of fleet; detour +7-10 days; Drewry Shanghai-Rotterdam +115%

items.hook: The most useful feature I built this year was a vocabulary I deleted.
items.body:
Early versions of ScoreMyBiz used the words I had used for eighteen years: debtors, creditors, receivables, accruals. Shopkeepers opened the app once and did not come back.

So it now says Sold, Bought, Spent, and who owes me. The maths underneath is unchanged. The daily use is not.

There is research behind this. Plain-language rewrites of government forms and bank letters raise completion and lower call volumes in every study I have seen. Finance has simply never applied it to its own customers.

Every profession keeps a dialect that holds outsiders at the door. If the person who needs the number cannot read its label, the number does not exist for them.
items.question: Which word in your management report would your best customer not understand?

items.hook: Wells Fargo set a target of eight products per customer. Staff opened 3.5 million accounts nobody asked for.
items.body:
Between 2009 and 2016 employees at Wells Fargo opened roughly 3.5 million deposit and card accounts without customer permission. The slogan was "eight is great". Hitting it decided commissions and, for many, whether they kept their job. About 5,300 people were dismissed.

This is Goodhart's law, named after a Bank of England economist in 1975 and sharpened later by Marilyn Strathern: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

It happens quietly in every plant and every finance team. Target on-time delivery and partial shipments go out. Target collection days and the sales team avoids slow but profitable customers.

Before you set next year's targets, ask the second question: what is the cheapest way to hit this number without doing the thing we actually want?
items.question: Which target in your company is being hit while its purpose is being missed?

card.title: Goodhart's law at Wells Fargo
points: Ask how the number can be gamed before you set it
card.stat_label: accounts opened without customer permission, 2009 to 2016
card.source: Wells Fargo disclosure, August 2017; Goodhart 1975

items.facts: Wells Fargo Aug 2017: 3.5 million potentially unauthorised accounts 2009-2016; 'eight is great' cross-sell target; ~5,300 employees fired; Goodhart 1975, Strathern phrasing

items.hook: If you pay a small supplier after 45 days, the tax department now disallows the expense for the year.
items.body:
Section 43B(h) of the Income Tax Act, in force from assessment year 2024-25: amounts owed to micro and small enterprises that are still unpaid beyond the MSMED Act limit on 31 March are not deductible in that year. The limit is 45 days with a written agreement, 15 days without one.

Medium enterprises are outside it. Only the supplier's Udyam classification matters, not your size.

And since the November 2024 notification, every company with turnover above 250 crore rupees had to be on a TReDS platform by 31 March 2025, so those suppliers can discount your invoices.

Before this year end: pull the creditor ageing, tag every Udyam-registered micro and small supplier, and clear anything older than 45 days before March. The cost of a late payment is no longer just a relationship.
items.question: Does your creditor ageing report show which suppliers are Udyam registered?

card.title: The 45-day rule
points: 45 days with a written agreement, 15 without
card.stat_label: after which a payment to a micro or small supplier loses its deduction
card.source: Finance Act 2023; MSME notification S.O. 4845(E), 7 Nov 2024

items.facts: S.43B(h) inserted by Finance Act 2023, AY 2024-25; MSMED s.15: 15 days or 45 days with written agreement; applies to outstanding at 31 March; TReDS threshold cut from Rs 500 cr to Rs 250 cr turnover, notification 7 Nov 2024, deadline 31 Mar 2025

items.hook: Experienced developers using AI tools were 19 percent slower. They believed they were 20 percent faster.
items.body:
METR ran a randomised trial in 2025 with 16 experienced open-source developers across 246 real tasks. Developers averaged five years and 1,500 commits on their projects.

With AI tools they took 19 percent longer. Before starting they expected to be 24 percent faster. After finishing, they still believed they had been 20 percent faster.

The lead author's explanation: suggestions were directionally right but not quite right, so time went into reviewing and correcting.

One study, early-2025 tools, so not the final word. But the gap between felt speed and measured speed is the real finding. If your team says AI is saving hours, measure the hours. The feeling is not evidence.
items.question: Have you measured an AI gain in your team, or only been told about it?

card.title: Felt speed versus measured speed
card.stat_label: slower with AI tools, experienced developers, measured
card.source: METR randomised controlled trial, 2025

items.facts: METR 2025 RCT: 16 developers, 246 tasks, +19% time with AI; predicted -24% before, believed -20% after; experts forecast -39%/-38%

items.hook: The naira lost about 70 percent of its value against the dollar in a year. Every Indian exporter to Nigeria learned what an unhedged receivable means.
items.body:
June 2023, the Central Bank of Nigeria let the currency float. On the first day the official rate moved from about 472 to 664 naira per dollar, a 41 percent fall. By mid 2024 the cumulative loss was close to 70 percent.

Companies with naira revenue and dollar costs reported currency losses that erased years of operating profit. Companies with dollar receivables and naira costs quietly became more competitive.

Where you sit on that line is a decision, even if you never made it consciously.

Three questions for any business with cross-border exposure: in which currency do we earn, in which do we spend, and how many months of mismatch can we survive? If the third answer is "fewer than six", you need a hedge, a price clause or a different customer.
items.question: Which currency mismatch is sitting in your business without a name on it?

card.title: Three questions on currency
points: In which currency do we earn?
How many months of mismatch can we survive?
Below six: hedge, clause or rethink
card.stat_label: naira against the dollar, June 2023 to mid 2024
card.source: BusinessDay, Bloomberg and FMDQ data; SEC filings

items.facts: Naira float June 2023; first day 471.67 -> 664.04 per USD (-40.78%); cumulative ~69-71% loss by mid-2024 (BusinessDay/Bloomberg, FMDQ, SEC filing 71% to June 2024)

items.hook: I approve far fewer spends than I used to. Three questions do the filtering.
items.body:
One: what decision changes if this works? If no decision changes, it is a vanity project with an invoice.

Two: what is the cheapest experiment that tells us? A pilot line before a plant. A landing page before a product. One district before a national launch.

Three: if it fails, what do we learn that we could not have learned for free? A failure with no lesson is just a cost.

This is not caution. It is the outside view applied to small money. Most spending is approved because the story is good, not because the evidence is. The questions force the evidence to show up first.
items.question: Which question would have stopped your most expensive mistake?

card.title: Three questions before any spend
points: What decision changes if this works?
What is the cheapest way to find out?

items.hook: Receivables are not a balance. They are a queue. And queues obey one law.
items.body:
Little's law, proved by John Little at MIT in 1961: the amount of work in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the time each item spends inside.

Apply it to money. Receivables equal daily sales multiplied by days sales outstanding. Stock equals daily consumption multiplied by days of cover. Work in progress equals daily output multiplied by cycle time.

Which means there are only two ways to shrink any of them: sell less, or shorten the time. Nobody chooses the first. So every working capital programme is really a time programme.

Sales of 2 lakh rupees a day at 60 days outstanding is 1.2 crore rupees in receivables. Cut to 45 days and 30 lakh rupees comes home without a single extra sale.
items.question: Which queue in your business is longest: receivables, stock, or work in progress?

card.title: Little's law for money
points: Receivables = daily sales x days outstanding
Stock = daily use x days of cover
WIP = daily output x cycle time
Shorten the time, free the cash
card.stat_label: work in system = arrival rate x time in system
card.source: John D.C. Little, Operations Research, 1961

items.facts: Little's law 1961 (Little, Operations Research 9(3)); worked example arithmetic: 2 lakh/day x 60 = 1.2 crore; x45 = 90 lakh, release 30 lakh

items.hook: Zero-based budgeting made Kraft Heinz the most efficient food company in America. Then it wrote off 15.4 billion dollars.
items.body:
February 2019. Kraft Heinz took a goodwill impairment of 15.4 billion dollars, mostly on the Kraft and Oscar Mayer brands, cut its dividend by 36 percent and disclosed an SEC inquiry into its procurement accounting.

Under 3G Capital every budget line had started from zero each year and had to justify itself. Margins rose fast. So did the quiet cuts to marketing, product development and the brand investment that sold ketchup in the first place.

Zero-based budgeting is a good tool. It finds the subscription nobody uses and the report nobody reads. It cannot tell you which cost is actually an investment with a slow return.

Use it on overheads. Protect the lines that create next year's revenue with a different rule: evidence of return, not absence of cost.
items.question: Which line in your budget looks like a cost but is really next year's revenue?

card.title: The Kraft Heinz lesson
points: Brand investment was cut like any cost
card.stat_label: goodwill write-down, February 2019
card.source: Kraft Heinz 2018 results, 21 Feb 2019; Boston Globe

items.facts: Kraft Heinz Feb 2019: $15.4bn goodwill impairment (Kraft, Oscar Mayer, other), dividend cut 36%, SEC procurement inquiry; 3G zero-based budgeting

items.hook: Two lawyers filed a brief with six court cases that did not exist. ChatGPT had invented them. The judge fined them 5,000 dollars.
items.body:
Mata v. Avianca, Southern District of New York, June 2023. The opposing lawyers could not find the cited judgments because there were none. The citations, the quotes and even the internal references had been generated.

Judge Castel's ruling is the useful part. Using AI is not improper. Failing to verify what you file is.

Now think about a board paper or an audit memo. A model will happily produce a confident paragraph on a tax ruling, a standard or a competitor's margin. Each one reads perfectly. Some are fiction.

The rule in my team: anything that cites a number, a case, a standard or a date is checked at source before it leaves. The drafting got faster. The checking got non-negotiable.
items.question: What is the last citation you put in a document without opening the source?

card.title: Verify before you file
points: Six invented cases in one brief
Fine: 5,000 dollars, and a public ruling
Using AI is fine. Not checking is not
Numbers, cases, standards, dates: check at source
card.stat_label: fabricated court cases in one filing
card.source: Mata v. Avianca, 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)

items.facts: Mata v Avianca sanctions 22 June 2023, Judge Castel; six fabricated cases; $5,000 fine on Schwartz, LoDuca and firm

items.hook: UPI handled 24.5 billion payments in one month. A shop that still refuses digital is refusing its customers.
items.body:
August 2026: 24.51 billion UPI transactions worth about 29.8 lakh crore rupees, per NPCI. Ten years after launch, monthly volume has grown nearly 13,000 times.

What this does to a small business is larger than convenience. Every digital sale is a timestamped record. The shop that takes UPI has, without trying, built a sales ledger a bank can read.

That is the quiet bridge over the credit gap. Cash leaves no trace and so earns no trust. Digital sales become a history, and a history becomes a loan.

For anyone advising small businesses: the first step toward credit is not an application form. It is six months of transactions that exist somewhere other than memory.
items.question: If a lender asked your business for six months of sales history tomorrow, where would it come from?

card.title: What a UPI record is worth
points: Every payment is a timestamped sale
A sales history is a credit history
card.stat_label: UPI transactions in August 2026
card.source: NPCI monthly statistics

items.facts: NPCI Aug 2026: 24.51 billion transactions, Rs 29.82 lakh crore; ~13,000-fold rise in 10 years (YourStory Aug 2026)

items.hook: After eighteen years of signing off numbers, I became a beginner. The hardest part was not the learning.
items.body:
Running finance for factories, I knew what every line in the P&L meant and who was hiding what in it.

Building an app for shopkeepers, I had to learn what "the month was good" means to a trader. It is rarely profit. It is whether she paid everyone and something was left.

The hard part was status. In a boardroom my questions carried weight. In a market my questions were ignored until I stopped sounding like an auditor.

There is research on this too. Experts underperform novices on problems just outside their field because expertise brings fixed frames. The frame that made me useful in one room made me useless in the next, until I put it down.
items.question: When did your expertise last get in the way of learning something?

card.title: Becoming a beginner again
points: The frame that helps in one room hurts in the next
Put it down before you can learn

items.hook: Most management mistakes come from using a complicated-problem method on a complex problem.
items.body:
Dave Snowden's Cynefin framework, published in Harvard Business Review in 2007, sorts situations into four kinds.

Clear: the answer is known, follow the procedure. Complicated: an expert can analyse it, like a machine breakdown or a tax computation. Complex: cause and effect only show afterwards, like a market entry or a culture change. Chaotic: act first to stop the bleeding, then think.

The error that costs most money is treating complex as complicated. We hire the consultant, build the model, present the plan, and are surprised when the market does not read it.

For complex problems the method is different: run small safe experiments, watch what happens, amplify what works. Cheaper, slower, and far more often right.
items.question: Which decision on your desk is complex, and which are you treating as merely complicated?

card.title: The Cynefin framework
card.source: Snowden and Boone, HBR November 2007

items.facts: Cynefin: Snowden & Boone 'A Leader's Framework for Decision Making' HBR Nov 2007; four domains (originally simple/complicated/complex/chaotic)

items.hook: Amazon's suppliers fund its growth. Its cash conversion cycle has been negative for years.
items.body:
Cash conversion cycle: days of inventory plus days of receivables minus days of payables. For most manufacturers it is 60 to 120 days of cash tied up before a sale turns back into money.

Amazon runs it negative, around minus 30 to minus 40 days in most years. Customers pay at checkout. Suppliers are paid weeks later. The business grows and the cash balance grows with it.

You do not need Amazon's scale to move in that direction. Collect at order for new customers. Negotiate payment terms that match your own collection cycle. Hold stock in days, not months.

Every day you cut from the cycle is cash you no longer have to borrow. At today's lending rates that is the cheapest money a CFO will ever find.
items.question: How many days is your cash conversion cycle, and when did you last compute it?

card.title: The cash conversion cycle
points: Inventory days + receivable days - payable days
Collect faster, pay on terms, hold less
Each day cut is cash not borrowed

card.source: Marketplace Pulse analysis of Amazon filings

items.hook: KPMG cut its UK graduate intake by 29 percent. Where will the partners of 2040 come from?
items.body:
UK reporting in 2025: KPMG's graduate scheme shrank from 1,399 to 942. Deloitte cut 18 percent, EY 11 percent, PwC 6 percent. Job adverts for accountancy graduates fell 44 percent against 2023.

The stated reason is AI doing the entry-level work. The unstated one is partner profit in a soft consulting market.

Here is the problem nobody in those firms has solved. The reconciliations, the schedules and the first drafts were tedious. They were also how every finance leader learned how the numbers connect.

If the machine does the junior work, training has to be redesigned, not removed. Juniors must review, challenge and explain from day one. The firms that do this keep their future partners. The others will have tools and nobody left who understands them.
items.question: How are you training people who will never do the work you learned on?

items.hook: More than three quarters of India's rain falls in four months. That is the real budget assumption behind every rural sales forecast.
items.body:
The southwest monsoon, June to September, delivers over 75 percent of India's annual rainfall. About 60 percent of farmland depends on it directly.

Agriculture is roughly 18 percent of GDP but close to half of all employment. A weak monsoon does not just hurt farmers. It shows up a quarter later in tractors, two-wheelers, cement, fertiliser, gold and the credit book of every kirana store in a district town.

Yet most corporate forecasts carry a single national demand number with no weather scenario in it.

The fix is not a meteorologist. It is two cases in the plan: normal monsoon and deficient monsoon, with rural volume, collections and credit terms adjusted for each. The IMD forecast in April tells you which case you are in.
items.question: Does your annual plan have a monsoon scenario, or just a number?

card.title: The monsoon in the forecast
points: Over 75 percent of annual rain in four months
Agriculture: near half of all employment
Plan two cases, pick one in April

card.source: India Meteorological Department; Infomerics 2025

items.facts: IMD/IITM: SW monsoon >75% of annual rainfall; Infomerics: ~60% of agriculture rain-fed, agriculture ~18% of GDP 2024, ~54% employment; Business Today 2026 ~46% employment

items.hook: I build for shopkeepers in India from a desk in Lagos. The distance turned out to be the product's best editor.
items.body:
Both cities run on small trade. Both have shop owners who know their cash to the last note and distrust anything calling itself finance.

Distance forces discipline. I cannot walk into a shop and explain a screen. The screen has to explain itself, in the words a trader uses, in the three seconds before she decides it is not for her.

Every feature goes through a test I could not have run from Mumbai: would this make sense to someone who has never met me and never will?

Constraints are not the enemy of good products. They are what stops a founder from shipping his own assumptions.
items.question: What constraint in your work turned out to improve the result?

items.hook: A fast-food chain tried for months to sell more milkshakes. Then it asked what job the milkshake was hired for.
items.body:
Clayton Christensen's jobs to be done, from his Harvard work: customers do not buy products, they hire them to make progress in a situation.

In his milkshake study, nearly half the shakes were bought early in the morning by commuters, alone, for a long drive. The competition was not another milkshake. It was a banana, a bagel, boredom.

Once the job was clear the improvements were obvious: thicker shake, faster counter, a card to skip the queue.

The shopkeeper does not want accounting software. He wants to know whether he can pay the supplier on Friday. The CFO does not want a dashboard. She wants to walk into the board without a surprise. Describe the job and the product simplifies itself.
items.question: What job is your customer really hiring you for, and who else is applying?

card.title: Jobs to be done
points: Find the situation, not the segment
Describe the job, simplify the product
card.source: Christensen, Hall, Dillon and Duncan, HBR September 2016

items.facts: Christensen et al 'Know Your Customers' Jobs to Be Done' HBR Sept 2016; milkshake study: ~40% of shakes sold early morning to commuters

items.hook: Holding ten crore rupees of stock costs two to three crore rupees a year. Most plants never see that invoice.
items.body:
Inventory carrying cost, the commonly used planning figure across supply chain bodies: 20 to 30 percent of average inventory value per year.

It is made of pieces nobody bills together. Cost of the capital tied up. Warehouse space and handling. Insurance. Obsolescence and damage. Shrinkage. The capital cost alone is usually the largest.

So when a plant manager asks for "a bit more safety stock", the question is not whether the warehouse has room. It is whether the service improvement is worth a quarter of the stock's value every year.

Put the carrying rate in the monthly pack next to the stock figure. Once people see the running cost, the stock conversation changes on its own.
items.question: What carrying rate does your company use, and is it in the monthly report?

card.title: The cost of holding stock
points: 20 to 30 percent of stock value a year
Show the rate next to the stock
card.stat_label: of inventory value, annual carrying cost, common planning figure
card.source: APQC and ISM benchmarks as cited in supply chain literature

items.facts: Carrying cost 20-30% of inventory value per year, commonly cited planning figure (APQC/ISM); APICS chapter rule of thumb 15-25%; 10 crore x 20-30% = 2-3 crore

items.hook: Pasting a customer list into a public AI tool is a data transfer under the DPDP Act. The penalty ceiling is 250 crore rupees.
items.body:
India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 treats a business that decides how personal data is used as a Data Fiduciary. Notice, consent or a listed legitimate use, purpose limitation and reasonable security safeguards are its obligations. A breach must be reported to the Data Protection Board and to the affected people. The schedule sets a ceiling of 250 crore rupees for failing security safeguards.

Now the finance team's habit: export the debtor ledger, paste into a chatbot, ask for a collections priority list. Names, phone numbers, amounts owed, straight to a third-party server, with no record of the transfer.

The fix is not banning AI. It is three rules. Anonymise before you paste. Use a tool under an enterprise agreement with no training on your data. Keep a log of what left the building. Then use the tool as much as you like.
items.question: Does anyone in your company know which customer data has already gone into a public AI tool?

card.title: AI and the DPDP Act
points: Personal data to a chatbot is a transfer
Breach: report to the Board and the people
Anonymise, enterprise tool, keep a log
card.stat_label: maximum penalty for failing reasonable security safeguards
card.source: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Schedule

items.facts: DPDP Act 2023: Data Fiduciary obligations s.4-8, breach intimation to Board and Data Principals s.8(6); Schedule penalty up to Rs 250 crore for failure of reasonable security safeguards; draft for lawyer review, not legal advice

items.hook: Scientists proposed a second time zone for India's northeast. It would save 20 million units of electricity a year. It was refused.
items.body:
In 2018 CSIR's National Physical Laboratory proposed IST-II, one hour ahead, for states east of 89 degrees 52 minutes, from Assam to Arunachal. The sun rises there well before Gujarat, yet offices open at the same clock hour and daylight is wasted in the morning and bought back as electricity in the evening.

The estimated saving was 20 million kilowatt-hours a year, plus a workforce whose body clock matched its working day.

It was turned down. The main reason was railway safety: every crossing between zones is a chance for a timetable error.

Every standard has winners and losers. One national clock is simpler for the centre and costly for the east. The question for a company is the same: which of your standards is simple for head office and expensive for the plant?
items.question: Which standard in your organisation is quietly paid for by the people furthest from head office?

card.title: One clock for a subcontinent
points: Sunrise differs by about two hours east to west
CSIR-NPL 2018: a second zone, one hour ahead
Estimated saving: 20 million units a year
card.stat_label: estimated annual electricity saving from IST-II
card.source: CSIR-NPL study, 2018, Current Science

items.facts: CSIR-NPL 2018 proposal: IST-I UTC+5:30 and IST-II UTC+6:30 east of 89°52'E; estimated 20 million kWh/yr savings; rejected citing railway safety; Gauhati HC dismissed PIL on DST committee advice

items.hook: The CIMA case study taught one habit I still use in every board paper: never give a recommendation without its implication.
items.body:
Not: exit the product line. Instead: exit the product line, expect revenue to fall by the line's contribution, release the working capital it holds, and watch the key account that buys it alongside everything else.

Boards do not pay for answers. They pay for the consequences you saw before they did.

The exam framework for this is simple: objective, position, proposal, implications, conclusion. It looks like exam technique. It is actually how a finance leader earns the right to be in the room when the decision is made rather than told about it afterwards.

I have seen bright analysts stall for years because they presented conclusions without consequences. The fix takes one extra paragraph.
items.question: What was the last recommendation you made without stating what it would cost?

items.hook: The side that learns faster wins, even when it is smaller. A fighter pilot proved it, and every business proves it again.
items.body:
John Boyd's OODA loop: observe, orient, decide, act, then observe again. His insight from air combat was that the pilot who completed the loop faster forced the other into reacting to a situation that had already changed.

In business the loop is the gap between a signal and a changed decision. Weekly numbers instead of monthly. A price revised in a day instead of a quarter. A product fix shipped before the complaint spreads.

Most large companies have an OODA loop measured in quarters because every step needs a committee. A smaller competitor with a weekly loop sees the same market twelve times as often.

The question for a finance team is not how accurate the monthly report is. It is how many decisions changed because of it, and how soon.
items.question: How long does it take your organisation to go from a signal to a changed decision?

card.title: The OODA loop
card.source: John Boyd, 'Patterns of Conflict', US Air Force briefings

items.hook: Same sales fall, two companies. One loses a little. One nearly dies. The difference was decided years earlier, in the cost structure.
items.body:
Operating leverage: the share of your costs that does not move with sales.

Worked example. Sales 100, variable costs 30, fixed costs 60, profit 10. Sales rise 10 percent: contribution rises 7, profit becomes 17, up 70 percent. Sales fall 10 percent: profit becomes 3, down 70 percent. A 10 percent swing in sales becomes a 70 percent swing in profit.

Now the same company with fixed costs of 30 and variable costs of 60. The same 10 percent fall takes profit from 10 to 6. Painful, survivable.

Every long lease, every permanent hire, every own-fleet decision raises the first number. Before you sign, run the 10 percent down case. The structure you choose in good years decides how much bad year you can survive.
items.question: What does a 10 percent fall in sales do to your profit, in numbers?

card.title: Operating leverage, worked
points: Run the down case before you commit
card.stat_label: profit swing from a 10 percent sales change at high fixed cost
card.source: Illustrative arithmetic

items.facts: Illustrative: contribution margin 70% so sales +/-10 changes profit by 7 on a base of 10 = 70%; alternative 40% contribution margin changes profit by 4

items.hook: AI on a messy ledger is a faster way to be wrong. The boring work comes first.
items.body:
Before any model, three unglamorous questions.

Is the chart of accounts consistent across entities, or does marketing sit in three different lines depending on who booked it? Are customer and supplier masters deduplicated, or does the same distributor exist four times with four credit limits? Does every plant book the same cost to the same line?

Fix those and even a spreadsheet looks intelligent. Skip them and the smartest model confidently reports nonsense, and because it is confident, people believe it.

I have never seen an AI project in finance fail on the model. They fail on master data, every time, usually six months after the demo.
items.question: Which data mess does your team work around every month instead of fixing?

card.title: Data before models
points: One chart of accounts, every entity
One master record per customer and supplier
Same cost, same line, every plant

items.hook: India's median age is about 29. China's is about 40. Japan's about 49. This is the biggest number in your hiring plan and it is not in it.
items.body:
United Nations population estimates put India's median age near 29 years, against roughly 40 for China and 49 for Japan.

The phrase is demographic dividend. The honest version is demographic window. It pays only if the young people have jobs, skills and the health to work, and most projections see the window narrowing in the 2040s.

For a company operating in India the implication is practical. Your labour pool is young, mobile and cheap to hire but expensive to keep. Training, not recruitment, is the constraint. For a company selling in Japan or China, the customer is ageing and so is the workforce that serves them.

Demography is slow, certain, and almost always missing from the five-year plan.
items.question: Does your five-year plan say anything about the age of the people who will work for you and buy from you?

card.title: Three median ages
points: A window, not a dividend, until the jobs exist
card.stat_label: India's median age, years, against about 40 in China
card.source: UN World Population Prospects 2024

items.facts: UN WPP 2024 approx: India 28.4-29.8, China ~39.6-41, Japan ~48-49; dividend window estimates 2041-2049

items.hook: Shopkeepers do not read financial statements. They read signals. So I stopped building statements.
items.body:
Is money coming in faster than it goes out? Who owes me and since when? Can I pay the supplier on Friday?

Those are the three questions a trader asks a hundred times a month. No balance sheet answers them in under a minute.

So ScoreMyBiz turns the daily entries into one score and a handful of plain warnings. The accountant in me resisted for a year. A score felt unserious. The shopkeepers in the market settled it: they looked at the score and ignored the statements.

The lesson travels. In most companies the monthly pack is forty pages and the board reads three numbers. Find the three. Lead with them. Keep the forty pages for the people who ask.
items.question: If your business had to be summarised in one number each morning, which would you choose?

items.hook: No serious accident has one cause. The Swiss cheese model explains why your controls fail together.
items.body:
James Reason's model from 1990: every safety layer is a slice of cheese with holes. An accident happens only when the holes in several slices line up at once.

A fraud in a finance department follows the same pattern. The maker-checker split was skipped because someone was on leave. The vendor master change needed no second approval. The bank reconciliation was two months behind. None alone would have let the money out. Together they did.

The useful discipline is not another slice. It is checking regularly whether the existing holes have drifted into line. Who is covering for whom this month? Which review has quietly become a formality?

Every control that is never tested is a slice you only think you have.
items.question: Which control in your business is currently covered by one person's good habits?

card.title: The Swiss cheese model
points: Failure needs the holes to align
Watch for drift, not just gaps
An untested control is a slice you do not have
card.source: James Reason, Human Error, 1990

items.facts: Reason 1990 Swiss cheese model, Human Error (Cambridge); applied to Reason's organisational accident model

items.hook: Southwest's fuel hedges earned 1.3 billion dollars in 2008. By December the same book was a 992 million dollar liability.
items.body:
Southwest Airlines hedged jet fuel further ahead than any rival. When oil spiked in 2008 its derivatives settled for 1.3 billion dollars of gains, cash basis, before profit sharing and tax.

Then oil collapsed. By 31 December 2008 the remaining hedge book stood at a net liability of about 992 million dollars, and the airline cut its hedged position to around 10 percent of expected consumption, locking in losses it would pay through 2011.

Both halves are the lesson. A hedge is not a bet that prices rise. It is a payment to make the future survivable whichever way it moves. If your treasury describes hedge gains as profit, it will one day describe hedge losses as a mistake, and the board will stop hedging at exactly the wrong moment.

Hedge to survive. Never to win.
items.question: Does your board see hedging results as insurance or as trading profit?

card.title: Hedge to survive, not to win
card.stat_label: Southwest fuel hedge gains in 2008, then a 992 million dollar liability
card.source: Southwest Airlines Form 10-K, fiscal 2008

items.facts: Southwest 10-K FY2008: $1.3bn settlement gains cash basis 2008 (up $566m); net hedge liability ~$992m at 31 Dec 2008; hedge reduced to ~10% of consumption 2009-2013

items.hook: Before buying any AI tool for finance, finish this sentence: the decision that changes is...
items.body:
If nobody in the room can finish it, the tool is a demo with a subscription.

Examples that pass. Pricing reviewed weekly instead of yearly because the margin analysis takes an hour, not a month. Credit limits set on live payment behaviour instead of last year's audited accounts. Stock reordered on actual sell-through instead of a planner's instinct.

Examples that fail. A dashboard that is prettier than the old one. A chatbot that answers questions nobody asked.

The research is consistent: productivity gains show up where the tool shortens a specific loop. So name the loop. Then measure, as the developer study showed, because felt speed and real speed are different things.
items.question: Which decision in your company would you most like to make faster, and what stops you today?

card.title: The decision test
points: Measure the hours, do not feel them

items.hook: It can cost more than 4,000 dollars to move a container 20 kilometres from Lagos port. That is roughly the price of shipping it from China.
items.body:
Apapa and Tin Can, the ports that feed Nigeria, were built for about 1,500 trucks a day and have handled over 5,000. The African Centre for Supply Chain estimated the congestion costs the economy 14.2 billion dollars a year. Clearing agents have reported four to six weeks for a container to get in.

For a finance team the lesson is in the landed cost sheet. The ocean freight line is the one everyone negotiates. The last 20 kilometres is the line that quietly doubles it.

I have watched budgets built on the China to Lagos rate collapse on the Apapa to Ikeja rate.

Wherever you operate: find the leg of your supply chain nobody has priced, because it is the one the plan assumes is free.
items.question: Which leg of your supply chain is missing from the landed cost sheet?

card.title: The last 20 kilometres
points: 14.2 billion dollars a year in congestion cost
Price the leg the plan assumes is free
card.stat_label: to truck a 40 foot container 20 km from Apapa
card.source: African Centre for Supply Chain; BusinessDay; Guardian Nigeria

items.facts: ACSC: $14.2bn/yr loss; ports built for 1,500 trucks/day handling ~5,000; >$4,000 per 40ft container for 20 km (BusinessDay); 4-6 weeks queue reported by clearing agents

items.hook: In the market nobody reads your profit and loss. Everyone knows whether you paid on the day.
items.body:
Reputation in small trade is a payment history. Suppliers extend credit to the shop that settles on the agreed day. Customers come back to the trader who never short-changed them. The whole thing runs on memory and word of mouth.

That is the oldest credit score in the world, and until recently nobody could see it except the people in the street.

Section 43B(h), UPI records, TReDS: India is slowly turning that street-level reputation into something a bank can read. The shopkeeper who paid on the day for twenty years finally has a way to prove it.

Everything I build tries to make that record visible to the person who earned it. The data was always there. It was just never written down.
items.question: Who do you trust in business because of twenty years of paying on time, with no paperwork at all?
items.facts: references S.43B(h), UPI, TReDS described in other items; no new figures

items.hook: Britain and France kept funding Concorde for years after both knew it would never pay. Economists named a fallacy after it.
items.body:
The sunk cost fallacy: continuing because of what has already been spent, not because of what will come back. The Concorde programme became its textbook case, kept alive through the 1960s and 70s by governments unwilling to write off the money already gone.

Every plant has a Concorde. The machine that never ran right and got one more overhaul. The software that needs one more module. The hire everyone is still waiting to see.

The money is gone whether you continue or stop. The only question is forward: from today, with what we now know, is this the best use of the next rupee?

A useful habit from capital review committees: ask the sponsor to re-propose the project as if it were new, with the remaining cost and the expected return. Most Concordes do not survive the re-proposal.
items.question: What are you still funding mainly because you already funded it?

card.title: The sunk cost test
points: The past spend is gone either way
Re-propose it as a new project
card.source: Arkes and Blumer, 1985; Concorde programme history

items.facts: Concorde: Anglo-French programme, commercial service 1976-2003, often called the Concorde fallacy (Dawkins & Carlisle 1976); Arkes & Blumer 1985 sunk cost psychology

items.hook: Before you extend credit to a distributor, four ratios will tell you more than his bank reference.
items.body:
Edward Altman's Z-score has predicted corporate distress since 1968. The version for private, non-manufacturing companies and emerging markets needs only the balance sheet and the profit and loss:

6.56 times working capital over total assets, plus 3.26 times retained earnings over total assets, plus 6.72 times operating profit over total assets, plus 1.05 times book equity over total liabilities.

Below 1.1 is the distress zone. Above 2.6 is safe. Between them is grey, where the model is least reliable and your own judgment matters most.

It is not a crystal ball. Asset-light businesses score oddly, and a single bad year can swing it. But as a first screen before a credit limit, it beats a reference letter and a handshake every time. Run it once a year on your ten largest customers.
items.question: When did you last recompute the credit risk of your largest customer, rather than assume it?

card.title: Altman Z-score, private company version
card.stat_label: distress and safe thresholds, Z double-prime
card.source: Altman, 1968 and later Z'' revision

items.facts: Altman Z'' (non-manufacturers/emerging markets): 6.56 WC/TA + 3.26 RE/TA + 6.72 EBIT/TA + 1.05 BVE/TL; zones distress <1.1, grey 1.1-2.6, safe >2.6; original 1968 model thresholds 1.81/2.99

items.hook: The reconciliation no machine can do is the one between the ledger and the warehouse floor.
items.body:
The system says stock is worth a certain amount. A walk through the warehouse says half of it has not moved since last year and the rest is damp.

The ledger says the customer owes you. The sales manager knows he is about to close his shop.

Matching numbers to numbers is now cheap. Bank to ledger, invoice to order, intercompany to intercompany: let the machine do all of it, and audit its exceptions.

Matching numbers to the world is the job that remains. It needs someone who walks the floor, calls the customer, and asks the operator why the scrap bin is full. The finance leaders who will be valuable in ten years are the ones who treat the walk as the work, not as a break from it.
items.question: When did a walk through the plant last change a number in your report?

card.title: Numbers versus reality
points: Numbers to the world: your job
Walk the floor, call the customer

items.hook: On 29 May 2023 Nigeria removed its petrol subsidy. Within two months the pump price had more than tripled. Every business learned pricing in a hurry.
items.body:
Petrol went from roughly 195 naira a litre to 617 by July. The subsidy had cost about 10 billion dollars in the previous year, so the removal was inevitable. The speed was not.

What happened inside companies is the useful part. Businesses that knew their fuel share of cost per unit repriced within days. Businesses that carried fuel inside a general overhead line discovered their margins had vanished a quarter later.

The same shock arrives elsewhere as a currency move, a tariff, a freight spike or a power tariff revision.

Preparation is one table: each major input, its share of unit cost, and the price change that would erase the margin. If you cannot fill it in from memory, fill it in this week.
items.question: Which input could triple in price tomorrow, and do you know its share of your unit cost?

card.title: When an input triples overnight
points: Petrol: about 195 to 617 naira a litre
Subsidy had cost about 10 billion dollars a year
Know each input's share of unit cost
card.stat_label: Nigerian petrol price, May to July 2023
card.source: Reuters and Al Jazeera, July 2023; NNPC pricing circulars

items.facts: Subsidy ended 29 May 2023; pump price ~N185-198 before, N617 at NNPC stations by 18 July 2023; subsidy cost ~$10bn the prior year (Reuters)

items.hook: As a plant finance head, three reconciliations saved me more money than every cost-cutting drive combined.
items.body:
One: physical stock to book, every month, by a team that does not report to the stores manager. Half the write-offs I ever found started as a variance somebody had been carrying forward.

Two: production output to power and raw material consumed. When yield moves and nobody can explain it, something is leaving the plant through a gate that is not the dispatch gate.

Three: customer ledger to the customer's own statement, quarterly, for the ten largest accounts. Disputes that surface at year end were visible in month two.

None of this is clever. All of it is boring. The discipline is doing it when nothing seems wrong, because the month it finds something is the month that pays for all the others.
items.question: Which reconciliation in your business is done only when something already looks wrong?

card.title: Three reconciliations that pay
points: Physical stock to book, independent team
Output to power and material consumed
Customer ledger to customer statement, top ten
Do them when nothing looks wrong
